stories.headline: Update: Trump Shifts to Economic Pressure on Iran, Admits No Direct Talks and Munitions Shortage
stories.summary:
President Trump has reversed course on Iran negotiations, telling Axios he is "low-keying it" and will rely on economic pressure rather than the threat of fresh military strikes to force a reopening of the Strait of Hormuz. Trump acknowledged the U.S. is only "semi-negotiating" with Tehran, walking back weeks of claims that a deal was imminent. Iran's foreign minister confirmed there are no direct talks, only indirect message exchanges through intermediaries.

The shift follows Iran's Supreme National Security Council issuing a sweeping list of demands Saturday — including full U.S. military withdrawal from the region, war damage reimbursement, and an end to the blockade and sanctions — which former Defense Secretary Mark Esper called "beyond the pale" and "ridiculous." Esper warned on ABC's This Week that Iran appears to believe it has the upper hand after more than five months of conflict.

Critics from both parties are questioning whether economic pressure alone can work. Former Israeli military intelligence official Danny Citrinowicz wrote that Iran has "spent decades operating under intense economic pressure" and has repeatedly shown it can absorb pain without abandoning core strategic interests. Reports also confirm U.S. stockpiles of premier offensive and defensive missiles are nearly exhausted after sustained strikes, limiting Trump's military options.

The Iran standoff carries enormous global economic stakes: oil prices have risen as the Strait of Hormuz, through which roughly 20% of the world's oil passes, remains closed. Trump's reliance on sanctions and a port blockade rather than military action represents a significant strategic pivot, with no clear timeline for resolution.

stories.headline: South Carolina Holds Senate Primary to Replace Lindsey Graham, With Foreign Policy Legacy on the Ballot
stories.summary:
South Carolina voters head to the polls Tuesday to choose a Republican Senate nominee to fill the seat of the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, who died of heart problems on July 11. The leading contenders are Graham's sister Darline Graham, appointed by the governor to fill the remainder of the term and now running for the full six-year seat, and Republican House members Ralph Norman and Russell Fry. The race is expected to be competitive enough that it may go to a runoff on August 25.

Analysts note the election marks a generational and philosophical inflection point for South Carolina's Senate delegation. Graham was one of Congress's most prominent foreign policy hawks, cultivating relationships with allied foreign leaders and championing U.S. military engagement abroad for more than two decades. None of the leading candidates has signaled any intention of following that path, and observers say South Carolina voters are not demanding it.

Graham's former staffers credit his repeated reelection victories less to his foreign policy profile than to his record of delivering federal resources to the state — including military installations, infrastructure funding, and the multi-decade dredging of the Port of Charleston to accommodate larger cargo vessels. That project is widely credited with transforming South Carolina's economy.

The outcome will affect the balance of the Senate and signal whether Republican primary voters in a deep-red state continue to reward institutionalist conservatives or prefer members who keep a narrower focus on domestic issues. A runoff, if triggered, would be held August 25.

stories.headline: Connecticut Democratic Primary Tests Chris Murphy's Influence Ahead of Potential 2028 Presidential Bid
stories.summary:
Connecticut Sen. Chris Murphy is putting his political capital on the line Tuesday in a Democratic House primary, backing 78-year-old Rep. John Larson against former Hartford Mayor Luke Bronin, 47, in what has become a closely watched test of Murphy's standing ahead of widely discussed 2028 presidential ambitions. The race in Connecticut's heavily Democratic 1st Congressional District features generational politics at its center, with Bronin arguing the district needs younger, more energetic leadership to counter the Trump administration.

Larson, who has served in the House since 1999 and is running for a 14th term, drew scrutiny last February when he froze on the House floor due to a complex partial seizure linked to a pre-existing heart condition. His campaign has leaned on his progressive voting record, including his push to impeach Trump, as well as Murphy's high-profile endorsement. Murphy told the Washington Examiner he backs Larson because of his effectiveness on gun violence funding and defense industry jobs.

Bronin's campaign has received financial backing from technology and AI sector donors, a contrast his opponents have highlighted. Murphy's team dismissed that support, with Larson's campaign manager calling Murphy's endorsement worth more than "all the AI data center billionaires behind Bronin combined." The race is also a four-way contest, increasing the odds that no candidate clears a decisive majority.

For Murphy, a Larson loss could complicate his national profile at a moment when Democratic primary voters have shown increasing willingness to replace veteran incumbents with younger challengers. Political strategists say a Larson victory would validate Murphy's endorsement and reinforce his status as a credible kingmaker within the party.

stories.headline: World's Oceans Hit Record-High Temperatures for July as El Niño Develops
stories.summary:
The world's oceans reached their hottest recorded temperatures for any July in history last month, according to the European Union's Copernicus Climate Change Service. The average sea surface temperature outside polar regions hit 20.96 degrees Celsius, surpassing the previous July record of 20.89 degrees Celsius set in 2023. July 2026 was also the joint second-warmest July on record globally, with temperatures 1.47 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial averages.

Scientists attribute the spike in part to developing El Niño conditions in the Pacific, a natural warming pattern that, combined with human-driven climate change, amplifies temperature extremes. Sea surface temperatures set records along Europe's Atlantic coast and in the western Mediterranean, contributing to widespread marine heatwaves. Western Europe recorded its hottest combined June and July on record, averaging 2.79 degrees Celsius above normal.

The consequences of ocean warming extend well beyond water temperatures. Warmer seas drive sea level rise through thermal expansion, intensify tropical storms and their rainfall, and have contributed to mass coral bleaching events worldwide. Scientists at the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts noted that dry soils across Western Europe — parched by an exceptional run of heat waves — have reduced the land's natural cooling capacity, further amplifying surface temperatures.

The data arrives as Western Europe contends with its fifth heat wave of the season and the United Kingdom braces for a potential official drought declaration. Copernicus researchers said the findings are consistent with projections that climate change is making extreme heat events both more frequent and more severe.

stories.headline: At Least 13 Killed as Ukraine Strikes Oil Refinery Deep Inside Russia's Tatarstan Region
stories.summary:
A Ukrainian drone strike on the city of Nizhnekamsk in Russia's Tatarstan republic killed at least 13 people — including one child — and injured 75 more, Russian officials said Monday. The attack, which lasted several hours overnight and into the morning, is among the deadliest single Ukrainian strikes on Russian soil since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion. Tatarstan's regional head declared a period of mourning.

Ukraine's Armed Forces confirmed that the Tanevo oil refinery in Nizhnekamsk was struck, and Ukrainian defense technology manufacturer FirePoint said its FP-1 drones were used in the attack. The city sits more than 1,100 kilometers from the Ukrainian border, underscoring Kyiv's expanding long-range strike capabilities. Russia's Investigative Committee said civilians uninvolved in military operations were among the victims; the BBC has not independently verified this claim.

Kyiv has not officially commented on the strike but has recently escalated attacks on Russian energy and logistics infrastructure it says funds Moscow's war effort. Russia simultaneously claimed its air defenses shot down more than 450 Ukrainian drones overnight. In a parallel development, five people were killed in a Russian artillery strike on Kharkiv, and Russian missiles also struck near Kyiv last week, killing 21.

The strike represents a significant escalation in the pattern of deep strikes inside Russia, raising questions about both the trajectory of the conflict and the vulnerability of Russian industrial infrastructure far from the front lines. Moscow condemned the attack on what it characterized as civilian areas, while Ukraine frames such strikes as legitimate targeting of war-sustaining economic assets.

stories.headline: Update: Typhoon Dolphin Forces Evacuation of Over One Million in Eastern China, Triggers Massive Disruptions
stories.summary:
Chinese authorities evacuated more than one million people from homes across eastern China, including parts of Shanghai, as Typhoon Dolphin made landfall Sunday in Zhejiang province with maximum sustained winds of 150 km/h (94 mph). Authorities issued their highest-level red alert for the storm, the strongest to hit China this year. Nearly 1,000 flights were cancelled in Shanghai alone, and major tourist attractions including parts of Disneyland and Legoland were closed.

Dolphin made two landfalls — first in Yuhuan and then in Wenzhou — before being downgraded to a tropical storm. Despite the downgrade, authorities warned of torrential rains, severe flooding, and landslide risks through Wednesday as the storm tracks north. Provinces including Shandong, Henan, Hubei, Anhui, Jiangsu, and Zhejiang face heavy rain forecasts, with some areas expected to receive 250–500mm over several days.

Wenzhou authorities relocated approximately 900,000 residents and opened more than 1,000 emergency shelters. In Taizhou, some 390,000 people were evacuated. A nine-year-old boy from Wenling is missing after reportedly being swept into the sea; Chinese officials have not announced confirmed casualties. Maritime authorities suspended passenger ferry routes and halted offshore construction projects along the Fujian coast.

The storm traveled an unusually long distance of 6,000 kilometers before landfall, giving it a lifespan more than three times that of an average typhoon and an exceptionally large circulation. Chinese state media reported that two people were detained for spreading AI-generated misinformation about the storm's damage on social media.

stories.headline: Wildfires Near Spokane Force 60,000 to Evacuate, Destroy at Least 600 Structures
stories.summary:
Fast-moving wildfires in and around Spokane, Washington — the state's second-largest city — forced the evacuation of approximately 60,000 people over the weekend and destroyed at least 600 homes, businesses, and other structures, authorities said Sunday. The fires burned roughly 8.2 square miles in the Spokane area and remained uncontained, with officials warning that dry weather in the coming days would sustain dangerous conditions. Evacuees included patients from a Veterans Affairs hospital in the city.

Across Washington state, approximately 390 square miles have burned, and dozens of additional wildfires stretched the capacity of federal, state, and local firefighting agencies. A separate fire that has burned nearly 525 square miles of grassland in western Idaho and eastern Oregon — threatening more than 600 homes and 800 other structures — entered its tenth day. No fatalities or missing persons had been confirmed as of Sunday, though officials cautioned it was early in the response.

Washington Governor Jay Inslee said he spoke with President Trump about the wildfires. U.S. Sen. Maria Cantwell, appearing at a news conference in Spokane with federal and state officials, warned that the region is not out of danger. Investigators had not yet determined the cause of the blazes.

The scale of the Spokane fires — in an urban and suburban setting — marks a significant escalation in the ongoing Western wildfire season. Aerial footage showed neighborhoods reduced to foundations with only chimneys remaining standing, drawing comparisons to previous urban wildfire disasters.

stories.headline: Western Europe Sets New Temperature Record as Continent Faces Fifth Heat Wave of Season
stories.summary:
France is bracing for its fifth heat wave alert of the summer season, with national weather agency Météo-France warning of temperatures approaching 40°C (104°F) in southeastern France beginning Tuesday. Across Western Europe, a prolonged stretch of extreme heat that began in May has contributed to major wildfires, record-breaking droughts, new national temperature records, and thousands of projected heat-related deaths. The average temperature for Western Europe's June-July period reached 21.62°C (70.92°F), breaking the previous record set in 2022, according to the European climate agency Copernicus.

July also saw the highest average sea surface temperature ever recorded for the month across ice-free oceans globally — 20.96°C (69.73°F) — surpassing the 2023 record. Scientists attribute the extreme conditions to a combination of accelerating human-caused climate change and a supersized El Niño weather pattern. Globally, 2026 is currently the third-hottest year on record behind 2024 and 2025, but scientists say there is an increasing chance it could become the hottest year ever recorded by December.

The Rhine and Danube rivers have both receded to historically low levels, with photos showing people walking on sandbars normally submerged beneath the rivers in Germany and Hungary. Climatologists warn that as soils dry out under prolonged heat, they lose their natural cooling capacity, creating a feedback loop that allows temperatures to build more readily.

The European heat emergency reflects a broader global trend, with scientists noting that extreme heat events that once occurred once per decade are now recurring multiple times per season across the continent. Public health authorities have urged residents — particularly the elderly — to stay indoors, as projections of excess mortality from the season continue to rise.
